The vessel is designed with sufficient head space to accommodate the volumetric expansion of sulfur as it transitions from solid to liquid state. The internal TES-HX configuration was designed using the validated CFD model discussed in Task 7 to meet the charge and discharge performance requirements defined under EOP-B and EOP-C. Thermal-hydraulic insights from the CFD analysis led to a design consisting of two serpentine flow paths installed symmetrically about the vertical diametral axis of the tank. This configuration ensures uniform heat transfer fluid flow distribution, promotes stable thermal stratification, and achieves the desired charge and discharge rates. The serpentine internal TES-HX design facilitates selective melting of sulfur from the top of the vessel to the bottom during initial melting and remelting after maintenance, allowing liquid sulfur to expand safely into the empty head space. A valve switching scheme was implemented to control HTF flow direction during charge and discharge operations, as schematically illustrated in Figure 2. During charging, hot HTF enters the internal TES-HX from the top of the vessel and exits from the bottom after transferring heat to sulfur. During discharge, the HTF flow direction is reversed such that cold HTF flows through the serpentine internal TES-HX from the bottom and exits as hot HTF at the top. This flow arrangement preserves thermocline formation within the vessel and maximizes exergetic efficiency. Comparative CFD simulations with reversed HTF flow directions showed a reduction in exergetic efficiency from 83.5% for the selected configuration to 75.1%, confirming the importance of HTF flow direction in system performance. The piping and instrumentation (P&ID) diagram of the system along with the instrumentation and sensors is shown in Figure 42. The system has three main loops: (a) thermal oil loop (shown in red) that is heated by the electric oil heater (E04) and stores thermal energy in sulfur heat storage vessel (E01) during charge mode, and retrieves heat from sulfur heat storage vessel during discharge mode, (b) pressurized hot water loop (shown in purple) that is heated by the hot thermal oil in a discharge heat exchanger (E06), which is then cooled by cooling water in a plate and frame heat exchanger sink (E05) to simulate industrial process heat load, and (c) cooling water loop (shown in blue) that is connected to the cooling tower (CT01) and operates during discharge mode. As illustrated in Figure 42, the system configuration includes temperature, pressure and flow sensors to make necessary measurements for performance measurement and verification.
